did_you_know.text: The name “Jordan” is probably related to the Hebrew root meaning “to go down,” because the river descends from the north to the Dead Sea. It is one of the best-known rivers in the land of Israel.
The expression “stiff-necked” comes from farming imagery: an animal that refuses to lower its head to accept a yoke. In the Bible, it describes people or a nation who stubbornly refuse to listen.
The number forty appears many times in the Bible and often marks a long period of preparation, testing, or change. The Flood and the spies’ journey are also associated with this number.
The phrase “the finger of God” is a vivid way of describing direct divine action, not a physical description. A similar expression appears in the story of the Ten Plagues.
The Hebrew word for “molten image” is related to a root meaning “to pour” or “to cast.” It describes a metal idol made by casting.

The names Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth-hattaavah preserve memories of events associated with them: burning, testing, and graves connected with craving. Place names thus kept memories of the wilderness journey alive.
Kadesh-barnea was probably located near the border between the Negev and northern Sinai. Its exact location is still debated by scholars.

Moses’ prayer is structured as an argument: he recalls the Exodus and the connection to the ancestors, but he does not claim that the people were innocent. It is an example of prayer grounded in responsibility and covenant memory.
Moses’ prayer also considers how other nations might interpret Israel’s exodus from Egypt. This shows that, in the Bible, national actions can have public and reputational significance.

The giant people called the Anakim also appear in the spy stories and in the account of the conquest of Hebron. Their name is therefore part of a broader tradition about giant peoples in Canaan, not an isolated detail.
